name: MPU-6050
title: Six-axis MEMS gyroscope and accelerometer with motion processor
summary: A motion sensor in a 4 × 4 × 0.9 mm QFN-24: a three-axis gyroscope (±250 to ±2000 º/s) and a three-axis accelerometer (±2 to ±16 g), each axis on its own 16-bit ADC, with a temperature sensor, a 1024-byte FIFO and an on-chip Digital Motion Processor. An auxiliary I2C master reads an external compass or other sensors for nine-axis fusion. It runs from 2.375 V to 3.46 V and draws 3.9 mA with everything on. The MPU-6050 is I2C-only with a separate VLOGIC I/O supply; the MPU-6000 adds SPI and uses VDD for its I/O.
key_figures: VDD 2.375 V to 3.46 V; VLOGIC 1.71 V to VDD (MPU-6050)
3.9 mA typ, all sensors and DMP; 5 µA idle

notes: Both are supplied on 5,000-piece reels.

circuits.title: Typical operating circuit, MPU-6050
circuits.description: Four capacitors complete the circuit. C1 filters the on-chip regulator at REGOUT, C3 holds the charge pump output at CPOUT, C2 decouples VDD and C4 decouples the separate I/O rail VLOGIC. SDA and SCL go to the host's I2C bus, AD0 picks one of two slave addresses, AUX_DA and AUX_CL lead out to the auxiliary sensor bus, and CLKIN, FSYNC and INT are the clock input, sync input and interrupt output. The NC and reserved pins stay open.

circuits.title: Typical operating circuit, MPU-6000
circuits.description: The MPU-6000 version of the same circuit. With no VLOGIC pin there is no C4; pin 8 is the SPI chip select /CS, and pins 9, 23 and 24 carry either I2C (AD0, SCL, SDA) or SPI (SDO, SCLK, SDI). C1 filters REGOUT, C2 decouples VDD and C3 holds CPOUT.

operation.text: One 4 × 4 × 0.9 mm QFN holds a three-axis MEMS gyroscope, a three-axis MEMS accelerometer, a temperature sensor and an on-chip Digital Motion Processor (DMP). Each of the six motion axes has its own 16-bit ADC, so the axes are sampled at the same instant. A second I2C port lets the chip read an external three-axis compass and so output nine-axis fused data; other non-inertial sensors such as pressure sensors can sit on that port too. The footprint matches the MPU-30X0 family.

The two parts are the same apart from the host interface. The MPU-6050 talks I2C only and has a VLOGIC pin that sets its I/O levels (1.71 V up to VDD; 1.8 V ±5 % or VDD in the specification tables). The MPU-6000 offers both I2C and SPI and runs its I/O from VDD, using pin 8 as the SPI chip select.

Three separate vibrating MEMS rate sensors detect rotation about X, Y and Z: Coriolis force on a driven structure shows up at a capacitive pickoff, and that pickoff signal is amplified, demodulated and low-pass filtered ahead of its ADC. Full scale is selectable at ±250, ±500, ±1000 or ±2000 º/s; the sample rate runs from 8000 down to 3.9 samples/s, with a selectable digital low-pass filter. Sensitivity is trimmed at the factory. The gyroscopes draw 3.6 mA and 5 µA in standby.

Each axis has its own proof mass whose displacement is sensed differentially by capacitors and converted by a dedicated sigma-delta ADC. Full scale is selectable at ±2, ±4, ±8 or ±16 g. Its scale factor is factory-trimmed and nominally does not change with supply voltage. Lying flat, the part reads 0 g on X and Y and +1 g on Z. The accelerometer alone draws 500 µA, and 10 µA to 140 µA in its low-power mode. It offers orientation and tap detection, user-programmable interrupts and a high-g interrupt.

The DMP runs motion-processing algorithms on the gyroscope, accelerometer and external sensor data so the host does not have to. Its results are read from its registers or through the FIFO, and it can drive an interrupt pin. Such algorithms usually want around 200 Hz to keep latency low even when the application itself updates as slowly as 5 Hz; the DMP keeps that loop off the host. It also supports a low-power pedometer that counts steps while the host sleeps. All six axes plus the DMP draw 3.9 mA.

The part is always a slave to the host. I2C reaches every register at up to 400 kHz (fast mode) or 100 kHz (standard mode). On the MPU-6000, SPI reaches every register at 1 MHz and the sensor and interrupt registers alone at 20 MHz. SPI and I2C share pins 9, 23 and 24. When the MPU-6000 is used on SPI, setting the I2C_IF_DIS bit soon after start-up keeps it from falling into I2C mode. The I/O level is VDD on the MPU-6000 and VLOGIC on the MPU-6050.

The bus is two open-drain lines, SDA and SCL, which need pull-ups. A transfer opens with START (SDA falls while SCL is high) and closes with STOP (SDA rises while SCL is high); a repeated START keeps the bus. Bytes are 8 bits, each answered by an acknowledge: the receiver holds SDA low through the ninth clock's high phase, and a not-acknowledge leaves it high. A slave may stretch SCL low while busy. To write, the host sends the address with W, then the register address, then one or more data bytes, the register address stepping on by one after each byte. To read, the host writes the register address, issues a repeated START with the address and R, takes one or more data bytes acknowledging all but the last, then NACK and STOP.

Four-wire SPI with the part as slave: SCLK, SDI and SDO are shared between slaves and each slave has its own active-low /CS; deselected slaves hold SDO high-impedance. Data travels MSB first, is latched on the rising SCLK edge and changes on the falling edge, with SCLK up to 1 MHz for full register access. A transaction is at least 16 clocks: the first byte is the R/W bit (1 = read) followed by a 7-bit register address, then one or more data bytes. Single and burst transfers are both supported.

AUX_DA and AUX_CL form a second I2C bus for an external magnetometer or other sensors. In master mode the chip reads those sensors itself so the DMP can fuse their data without the host; it can burst-read up to 24 bytes from up to four sensors, plus single-byte reads and writes to a fifth (slave 4). In pass-through mode its own master logic is switched out and analog switches join AUX_DA and AUX_CL to the primary SDA and SCL, so the host talks to the external sensors directly while still reaching the chip. Pass-through is used to configure the external sensors, or to let the chip stay in low power while just the external sensors are in use. The chip's master is limited and relies on the host to configure the auxiliary sensors first, after which the bypass is turned off. On the MPU-6000 in SPI mode the bypass is not reachable, so the external sensors are configured through slaves 0 to 4 instead; results from slaves 0 to 3 can go to the FIFO and the external sensor registers.
On the MPU-6000 the auxiliary bus runs at VDD. On the MPU-6050 AUX_VDDIO selects the level and must be 0, its reset value; then every logic pin, the auxiliary pair included, is referred to VLOGIC.

An on-chip PLL makes the internal clock from one of several sources: an internal relaxation oscillator, the MEMS oscillator of the X, Y or Z gyroscope (±1 % over temperature), or an external 32.768 kHz or 19.2 MHz square wave at CLKIN. The chip starts on its internal oscillator and stays there until told otherwise, so the gyroscopes can settle before one is chosen. The relaxation oscillator suits low-power modes with the gyroscopes off; a gyroscope source is more accurate when they run. Clock error goes straight into the DMP's distance and angle results.

Read-only registers hold the newest gyroscope, accelerometer, auxiliary sensor and temperature readings and may be read at any time; an interrupt can flag new data. A 1024-byte FIFO, set up by its configuration register, can collect any mix of gyroscope, accelerometer, temperature, auxiliary sensor and FSYNC data, with a counter giving how many valid bytes it holds. It supports burst reads, so the host can sleep between bursts.

INT can be push-pull or open-drain, latched or pulsed (50 µs with LATCH_INT_EN = 0), with a choice of how it clears. Sources are enabled one by one and flagged in the interrupt status register: the clock generator locking to a new reference, new data ready, accelerometer events, FIFO overflow, I2C master errors (lost arbitration, NACK from an auxiliary sensor) and I2C slave 4.
An on-chip sensor and ADC measure die temperature; the host gets the result from the sensor data registers or the FIFO. The temperature channel has its own programmable digital filter.

The bias and LDO block makes the internal supplies and references from an unregulated VDD of 2.375 V to 3.46 V and, on the MPU-6050, from VLOGIC; its output is decoupled at REGOUT. A charge pump makes the high voltage the MEMS oscillators need and is decoupled at CPOUT. The capacitors are C1 and C3 in the external components table.
VDD rises from 10 % to 90 % in no more than 100 ms and VLOGIC in no more than 3 ms, both monotonically. VLOGIC starts rising no earlier than VDD and never exceeds it.

Self-test registers 13 to 16 actuate each gyroscope and accelerometer axis electrically, exercising both its mechanics and electronics. The difference between the outputs with and without self-test is the self-test response, and it must lie within the relative limits of −14 % to 14 % from factory trim. The limits apply to Revision D parts with date code 1147 (YYWW) or later.

In top view with pin 1 at the upper left and pins 1 to 6 down the left side, +X points right, +Y points towards pins 19 to 24, and +Z points out of the top face. Each axis also carries a positive sense of rotation about it.
The exposed die pad has no electrical connection and is not needed for heat. Leave it unsoldered: soldering it can shift performance through thermo-mechanical stress.

A gyroscope also senses stress from the PCB: a mismatch in thermal expansion between package and board shifts the offset and its drift over temperature. Keep the traces to the pads as symmetric as possible so the part self-aligns and the solder joints come out even. Use lead-free solder and RoHS-clean materials.

No traces or vias run under the package where they would pass beneath the exposed pad. The gyroscopes are driven near X = 33 ±3 kHz, Y = 30 ±3 kHz and Z = 27 ±3 kHz, and active signals in unshielded layers directly above or below can couple into them at harmonics. A ground plane under the pad cuts board noise; if another board stacks over the part, a ground plane on it directly above the part shields it.
Keep large insertion parts such as buttons, connectors and shield cans at least 6 mm from the part.

If the package sits rotated against the board axes, each axis picks up a share of motion about the others equal to the sine of the error. The cross-axis figures in the gyroscope and accelerometer tables already include the die's own misalignment in the package.

The part is qualified to 10,000 g shock, but a drop onto a hard floor, or snapping boards apart by hand, can exceed that. Ultrasonic cleaning can damage it through resonance. Handle it as ESD-sensitive: keep it in its moisture-sealed ESD bag until assembly and work at stations held under 200 V of static.

Qualified to IPC/JEDEC J-STD-020D.1 with three reflow passes after bake and moisture soak, peak classification temperature 260 +5/−0 °C for lead-free parts under 1.6 mm thick. Ramp-up stays under 3 °C/s and ramp-down under 4 °C/s; preheat 60 to 120 s; 60 to 120 s above liquidus; 10 to 30 s near peak; under 480 s from room to peak. For production a lower-peak lead-free solder (about 235 °C) and gentler ramps are preferred, never beyond the qualification profile.
Moisture sensitivity level 3.
The top carries INVENSENSE, the part number (MPU6000 or MPU6050), a lot traceability code, and a line with foundry code, package vendor code, year and work week (YYWW) and revision code.
5,000 parts on a 330 mm reel, one reel per box, up to five boxes (25,000 parts) per carton. Reels ship in a vacuum-sealed moisture barrier bag with ESD, MSL3 and caution labels.
RoHS and Green compliant; the MEMS element is sealed hermetically by wafer-level bonding.
